Pre-Independent 2 · Unit 4 · Beyond Words

Class 3 · Infinitives in action

Review what you already know, discover three more uses of to + base verb, and use the language to communicate more clearly.

Today's mission

Use infinitives to say more

Last class, you practised infinitives after certain verbs. Today, you will review that pattern and add three more: after adjectives, after a verb + object, and to explain purpose.

Review

We want to understand.

After adjectives

It's important to listen.

Verb + object

I asked her to repeat it.

Purpose

I called to ask a question.

Learning goals

  • Recognise and use four common patterns with to + base verb.
  • Take notes while listening and notice adjective + infinitive patterns.
  • Practise the patterns through short interactive challenges.
  • Use the language in a pair interview and an improved oral presentation.
Teacher note

The listening activity uses the audio provided for this class. For reliable playback, download and extract the ZIP file, keeping the HTML and MP3 in the same folder.

Part 1 · Review in a new way

Conversation rescue

Last class, you practised verbs followed by to + base verb. Now help people finish real-life messages. This is not a multiple-choice quiz: read the situation, create a sentence aloud with a partner, then reveal a possible answer.

Partner challengeChallenge 1 of 6
Situation

Your friend has a problem.

Use “want” to say what your friend wants to do.

Teacher tip: invite students to suggest their own answers before revealing the model. Accept other grammatically correct answers.

Pattern reminder

want / need / hope + to + verb

I want to explain.

decide / plan / agree + to + verb

We decided to talk.

Part 2 · New use 1

To-infinitive after adjectives

Use adjective + to + base verb to describe feelings, reactions, or how easy/difficult something is.

Feelings / reactions

I'm happy to help.

I'm sorry to hear that.

We're excited to start.

Difficulty / evaluation

It's hard to understand.

It's easy to forget.

It's important to listen.

Notice the pattern

In these sentences, the adjective describes a feeling or evaluation. The infinitive tells us what causes the feeling or what action is being described.

Pattern: subject + be + adjective + to + base verb
It is difficult to find time. / I am glad to hear that.

Listening lab · Listen and take notes

Listen to the conversations. Your job is to notice the language patterns—not to fill in blanks. While listening, note the adjective or expression and the infinitive that follows it. Play the audio more than once if needed.

Before revealing the transcript, compare your notes with a partner. Underline the adjective or expression and circle the infinitive in each example.

Listen → notice → explain

Transcript · Conversation 1

Man: Jess, I am sorry to hear you are leaving us.

Woman: Yeah, I will miss this place.

Man: Where are you going next?

Woman: I am going back to college to get my PhD.

Man: Well, we will miss you.

Woman: Thanks. I am sad to leave this place, but I am excited for a new start.

Man: Well, we are sad to see you go, but best of luck with your studies.

Woman: Thanks. I appreciate that.

Transcript · Conversation 2

Woman: How was the game?

Man: It was good. I am happy to hear we finally won.

Woman: Oh, great. I am glad to hear that.

Man: Yeah, it was nice to win for a change.

Woman: Yeah, it's no fun to lose.

Man: It certainly is not.

Transcript · Conversation 3

Woman: So, how is the diet going?

Man: Not good. It is so hard to lose weight.

Woman: I know. It is never easy to stick to a diet.

Man: Also, I am very busy, so it is hard to find time to exercise.

Woman: Well, don't give up. You can do it.

Man: That's easy for you to say. You never gain weight.

Feedback · What should you notice?

  • Common pattern: be + adjective + to + base verb: sorry to hear, sad to leave, happy to hear, glad to hear.
  • Expressions with It is + adjective + to + verb: It is hard to lose weight. It is easy to stick to a diet.
  • No fun to lose is a negative evaluation: the speaker says losing is not enjoyable.
  • In easy for you to say, you identifies the person doing the action, and to say is the infinitive.
Check your notes: Can you explain the pattern in your own words? Give one new example that was not in the audio.

Quick practice · Choose the natural sentence

Round 1 of 8
Part 3 · New use 2

Verb + object + to-infinitive

Use this structure when one person asks, tells, invites, reminds, or wants another person to do something.

verb + person + to + base verb

I asked him to repeat the message.

She told us to wait.

They invited me to join the team.

My friend reminded me to call.

My teacher wants me to practise.

We encouraged her to speak.

My parents allow me to go out with friends.

He warned us not to touch the equipment.

Remember the object!

Compare:

✓ “I want to leave.” (same person wants and leaves)

✓ “I want you to leave.” (I want another person to leave)

✗ “I asked him repeat it.” → ✓ “I asked him to repeat it.”

Part 4 · New use 3

To-infinitive to express purpose

Use to + base verb to explain why someone does something. Ask yourself: Why?

I called to ask a question.

Why did I call? To ask a question.

She went online to find information.

Why did she go online? To find information.

We practise to improve.

Why do we practise? To improve.

She saved money to buy a laptop.

He went to the kitchen to get some water.

Purpose or result?

Here, the infinitive explains the intention or reason for the action, not necessarily the result.

“I sent a message to apologise.” = apologising was the purpose of sending it.

Part 6 · Speaking workshop

Say it, then ask it

Use the infinitives to talk about your communication, preferences and goals. Prepare ideas first, then turn them into questions for a partner.

Step 1 · Complete your ideas

Write short, true sentences. Try to use a different infinitive pattern each time.

Step 2 · Turn the idea into a question

Statement

“I want to learn a new skill.”

Question

“What do you want to learn?”

Statement

“It is important to be honest.”

Question

“What is important when you communicate?”

Don't simply add a question mark. Change the sentence so it asks your partner for information.

Step 3 · Breakout-room interview

In pairs: Student A asks three questions. Student B answers with details and a follow-up question. Then switch roles.

  • What do you want to improve about your communication?
  • What is difficult for you to do in English?
  • Who do you ask to help you when you have a problem?
  • What do you use your phone to do most often?
  • What is important to you in a good friend?
  • What would you like to learn to do this year?

Useful follow-ups: Why? / Can you give an example? / How do you feel about that?

Part 7 · Two-draft challenge

Can you improve your presentation?

Topic: “What makes someone a good communicator?” First try it your way. Then learn a simple structure and present a stronger version.

Version 1 · First attempt

Do it your way

Prepare a 45–60 second presentation without reading the tips below. Speak from your own ideas. Don't worry about perfection yet.

Teacher: give students 3–4 minutes to prepare. Invite volunteers to present. Listeners should listen without correcting yet.

Mini-lesson · Build a better talk

Four steps for a clearer presentation

  1. Opening: state your topic.
    “Today, I'd like to talk about what makes someone a good communicator.”
  2. Give two clear points.
    “First, a good communicator listens carefully. Also, it is important to be honest.”
  3. Add an example.
    “For example, I try to listen without interrupting when my friend has a problem.”
  4. Finish with a conclusion.
    “To sum up, good communication helps people understand and trust each other.”
Grammar goal: include at least two patterns with to + base verb, e.g. “It is important to listen” and “I asked my friend to explain.”
Version 2 · Improved attempt

Plan, practise, present again

Exit ticket

One idea to take away

Complete these three quick reflections before you leave.

Remember

to + base verb can follow certain verbs, adjectives, a person/object after some verbs, or explain the purpose of an action. Look at the words before the infinitive to recognise the pattern.
